description: We are AstroQué, a team of software engineering students from the Universidad Científica del Sur who are passionate about programming, design, and space exploration. For the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Map of Mars” challenge, we will develop an interactive app using real NASA data on Martian terrain, climate, and hazards to plan safe missions.
summary: MarsWalk (“Plan it safely. Bring back the science”) is a browser-based, serverless extravehicular activity (EVA) planner designed for human exploration of the western part of Jezero Crater on Mars. Developed using datasets from multiple NASA and USGS missions, it answers three fundamental questions on a single screen: where to walk (an A* pathfinding algorithm calibrated to Mars’ planetary radius that avoids steep cliffs, validated by HiRISE, while enforcing a 10-km return radius), when to go (typical surface weather conditions, both seasonal and hourly, based on Perseverance’s MEDA, as well as radiation dose context from Curiosity’s RAD), and why to go (selected geological stops with scientific information and uncropped surface images from Mastcam-Z).
details:
Live app: https://berrospijaviermayermelito-hub.github.io/MarsWalk/web/

Repository and documentation: https://github.com/berrospijaviermayermelito-hub/MarsWalk

Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MYktgqRbwQQ

WHAT IT DOES

MarsWalk is a web planner for a human walk (EVA) in the western part of Jezero crater, where NASA's Perseverance rover landed on February 18, 2021. One screen answers three questions:

- Where do I walk? An automatic safest route (A* algorithm) from the habitat through three science stops and back, avoiding steep and rough terrain.

- When do I go? Typical air temperature, ground temperature, pressure and wind measured by Perseverance (MEDA), for any season and hour of the Martian day, plus the radiation dose for the planned EVA.

- Why do I go? Three science stops chosen from NASA Mars Trek points of interest (Séítah, the delta front and Belva crater), each with NASA's own description and a real Perseverance Mastcam-Z photo taken at that spot.

HOW IT WORKS

- Terrain: we computed slope and roughness from the USGS/NASA Mars 2020 CTX elevation model (20 m/px) and built a cost grid of about 60 m cells.

- Safety rules from published sources: slopes up to 20° (NASA requirement HLS-S-R-0071 for suited astronauts), with cells blocked above 15° as a safety margin; a 10 km walk-back limit from the habitat (NASA JSC Walkback Test); 3.4 km/h walking speed in Mars gravity (Cavagna et al., Nature, 1998); a 6 h nominal EVA (NASA NTRS 20210026296).

- Weather: typical values from 148 sols of Perseverance MEDA data in the NASA Planetary Data System, by season and local hour (median and 10th–90th percentiles). It is not a forecast.

- Radiation: reference dose rate measured by Curiosity's RAD (about 210 µGy per day, NASA PIA17600), multiplied by the EVA duration. When the user adds time at each stop, the EVA clock and the dose update live, and the app warns when the 6 h limit is exceeded.

- A guided "Start EVA" mode walks through the route stop by stop, with an elevation profile.

VALIDATION

- We compared our slope map with an independent HiRISE 1 m elevation model: mean difference 0.05°, RMSE 2.5°. Because the 20 m model smooths short scarps, we block at 15°, which catches 88% of the cells HiRISE shows as steeper than 20°.

- We checked the map against Perseverance's real traverse (NASA data, 332 drives, 27.2 km): 98.3% of the rover's path lies on terrain we mark as walkable.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

MarsWalk turns orbital and rover data from several NASA missions (MRO, Mars 2020, Mars Science Laboratory, Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Odyssey, Viking) into one decision tool for planning a safe and scientifically useful Mars walk. It also shows the limits of the data openly, so planners know what the map cannot see.

CREATIVITY

Instead of showing data layers side by side, MarsWalk combines them into a single plan and tests itself against reality: the route is checked against a higher-resolution model and against the path NASA actually drove, and every science stop is a place Perseverance really visited.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Every number in the app has a cited source (DATA_SOURCES.md); we did not invent values. The time at each stop has no published value, so it is a user input.

- Honest limitations: the slope, walk-back and EVA limits come from lunar studies; the walking speed was measured without a spacesuit; the radiation value was measured in Gale crater, not Jezero; sand and objects smaller than 20 m are not resolved.

- Reliability: a local copy of the map tiles is used if NASA Mars Trek is unreachable.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, Rasterio, Matplotlib, Pillow) for data processing; JavaScript with Leaflet 1.9.4 and Chart.js 4.4.1 for the web app; GitHub Pages for hosting. All code is open source under the MIT License. AI assistance is stated in the README ("Use of AI") and in the metadata of every data file.
